opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say up front that "optimistic" is a relative term. I'm not one of the people who thinks we've got this all figured out, and I'm also not one of the people who thinks we're all doomed. But the reason for my reasonable optimism, if I can put it that way, is pretty simple: for most of its history, AI safety was a field that had to proceed almost entirely by philosophical argument. People were reasoning about hypothetical superintelligences that didn't exist, and it's very hard to make steady progress when you have no experiments to run and nothing to check your ideas against.

That's changed. We now have systems like GPT and its successors that are powerful enough to be genuinely interesting, and in some ways genuinely concerning, but not so powerful that we can't study them. So for the first time, AI safety can become an empirical science. You can try an alignment technique and see whether it works. You can try to get a model to misbehave and measure how often it does. And as a theoretical computer scientist, I find that exciting, because the history of science suggests that once you have that feedback loop between theory and experiment, things start to move.

Let me give a few concrete examples of why I think near-term progress is achievable. One is interpretability. These neural networks are often described as black boxes, but they're actually the most transparent black boxes you could ask for. You can see every weight and every activation, and you can intervene on them however you like. Compare that to neuroscience, where you're trying to understand a brain you can barely probe. People in interpretability are already finding meaningful internal structures, things like directions in activation space that correspond to truthfulness or particular concepts. It's early, but it's real.

Another example is something I worked on during my time at OpenAI, which is watermarking the outputs of language models. The idea is that you subtly bias the model's choice of words using a pseudorandom function, in a way that's invisible to a human reader but statistically detectable by someone who holds the key. That doesn't solve alignment, obviously, but it addresses a very concrete near-term problem: knowing whether a piece of text came from an AI, for things like academic dishonesty, propaganda, or spam. It shows that there are well-defined, mathematically tractable problems in this space where you can actually prove things.

And more broadly, I like the idea, which goes back to ideas in complexity theory, that a weaker verifier can sometimes check the work of a much more powerful prover. Interactive proofs are exactly about that. Whether that kind of insight can be turned into practical ways for humans to supervise systems smarter than us is a wide-open question, but it's the kind of question where theoretical computer science might have something to contribute.

So my optimism is really about the near to medium term. Can we make measurable progress on problems like these, problems with clear definitions and experiments we can run? I think the answer is yes. Whether that's ultimately sufficient for what happens if and when we build systems far more capable than us, that's the harder question, and I try to be honest that I don't know. But I'd much rather be working on problems where we can make progress than just wringing our hands.

r001.rationale: It says alignment techniques can be tried and their effectiveness measured, presenting that experimentation as a way to learn.

r002.rationale: It contrasts AI safety’s earlier reliance on philosophical arguments about hypothetical systems with the new ability to run experiments on existing models.

r003.rationale: It gives no argument based on the software industry thriving despite easy piracy.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say up front that I'm a theoretical computer scientist by background, I spent most of my career working on quantum computing and computational complexity, and I only came to AI safety relatively recently, when I spent a couple of years at OpenAI. So I don't come to this as someone who's been immersed in the alignment discourse for decades. But I think that outsider perspective is actually part of why I'm somewhat optimistic, or at least less pessimistic than some people.

The thing that really changed my view was that, for a long time, AI safety was almost entirely a philosophical and theoretical enterprise. People were speculating about what a superintelligent agent would do, how it would reason about its own goals, and so on, with essentially no empirical foothold at all. And it's very hard to make progress on anything when you can't run experiments. But now we actually have these systems. We have large language models that are, in many respects, surprisingly capable, and crucially, they're not the alien paperclip maximizers that a lot of the earlier thinking assumed. They were trained on the entirety of human writing, so they come out of the box with a kind of familiarity with human values, human concepts, human norms. That doesn't mean they're aligned, of course, but it means the problem looks different, and in some ways more tractable, than the version people were worried about fifteen years ago.

So now you can ask concrete questions. Can you detect when a model is being deceptive? Can you interpret what's going on inside the network? Can you build in watermarking so that AI-generated text is distinguishable from human text, which was actually the main thing I worked on at OpenAI? These are things where you can make incremental progress, you can measure whether you've made progress, and you can publish results that other people can build on. That's the kind of problem that science is actually good at.

The other thing I'd say is that there's a dangerous ambiguity in the phrase "AI safety." People use it to mean everything from, will this chatbot say something racist, to, will this thing kill all of us. And I think the near-term problems, the ones about misuse, about misinformation, about people being deceived or manipulated, those are problems where I'm pretty confident we can make real headway, because they're continuous with problems we've dealt with before. The existential questions, I'm much less sure about. I don't think anyone knows how to solve those. But I've become more hopeful that the work we do on the near-term problems will actually teach us things that are relevant to the longer-term ones, rather than being a distraction from them. And that's a view I didn't hold going in.

r001.rationale: The response says concrete safety research can be measured and that near-term work may teach us about longer-term problems, but it does not identify deploying safety measures as the way to learn.

r002.rationale: It describes earlier AI safety as largely philosophical and theoretical, with essentially no empirical foothold, and says current systems now make experiments possible.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention software piracy or use the software industry’s experience with piracy as grounds for optimism about managing AI misuse.

astra-6.text:
Well, I’m reasonably optimistic because there are a lot of concrete things we can try. We don’t have to solve the entire philosophical problem of what human values are before we can make progress on understanding why a model gives a particular answer, testing whether it behaves deceptively, or making it harder to bypass its safeguards.

And we have systems today that we can actually experiment with. You can propose a safety measure, try to break it, learn from the failure, and improve it. That feedback loop is enormously valuable. AI itself might also help us check code, find vulnerabilities, and understand other AI systems.

Now, none of that guarantees that techniques that work today will scale to a superintelligent system. That’s a much harder question, and I don’t think anyone knows the answer. But there’s a difference between saying we don’t have a guaranteed solution and saying there’s no useful work to do. In the near to medium term, I see plenty of useful work to do, and plenty of opportunities to find out empirically what works.

r001.rationale: It says safety measures can be tried on current systems, tested, and improved based on failures, identifying experimentation with safety measures as a way to learn.

r002.rationale: It describes empirical testing as useful but does not say AI safety is becoming empirical after decades of armchair speculation.

r003.rationale: It gives no software-industry or piracy-based argument about managing AI misuse.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I’m reasonably optimistic because there are a lot of concrete questions here where we can actually do experiments and learn something. We don’t have to solve the entire philosophical problem of what human beings ultimately want before we can make progress on understanding why a model behaves the way it does, or whether a particular safeguard works.

And with the systems we have today, you can try an approach, find out how it fails, and improve it. You can study whether a model is being deceptive, whether it follows instructions in situations different from the ones it was trained on, and how easily its safeguards can be circumvented. That gives researchers something to get their hands on.

Now, that’s a reason for optimism about making progress. It’s not a guarantee that progress will be fast enough, or that the techniques that work today will continue to work for much more capable systems. But I think there’s a substantial amount of useful scientific work we can do right now, and that seems like a much better position than simply having to speculate about the whole problem.

r001.rationale: It describes trying safeguards on current systems, observing how they work or fail, and improving them to learn about safety.

r002.rationale: It supports empirical research, but does not say safety has become empirical after decades of armchair speculation.

r003.rationale: It gives no software piracy analogy or related argument about managing AI misuse.
